So, Mr. Speaker, when we analyse the contention that taxation has been reduced we find that the record of the government does not support that claim.
There was one reference in the budget speech which to me was rather surprising; I refer to the remarks of the minister concerning the tourist trade. The government would appear to suggest that it is entitled to some credit in respect of the great advantage accruing to Canada through the vast amount of money spent in this country by the tourists. What has this government done to encourage the tourist trade throughout this country? It has two opportunities to extend some aid in the construction of highways, and everyone knows that highways are the first requisite, the first attraction and the most important element in the development of tourist traffic. On two occasions this government emphatically rejected the opportunity to assist the tourist trade in this way. Undoubtedly the provinces are aware of the advantage of this

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
trade and are looking after it, but they are doing so at their own expense, on their own account and without any assistance or encouragement from this government.
The sales tax is now reduced. If the government had accepted the resolution presented from this side of the house the sales tax would have been wiped out entirely. It is just as much trouble and expense to business to collect the amount of tax now imposed as it was to collect the larger amount, and it seems to me the government would have been well advised to do away with this tax completely. It is more or less a nuisance tax; it is an encumbrance, an obstruction to business, and the effect of wiping it out would have been borne equally and fairly by all the people of Canada. When the government took off the tax on luxuries, sleeping car tickets and the like, they were doing something for a particular class of people, but had they taken off the sales tax entirely they would have done somthing for every class throughout Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we come to the customs tariff, and it is here that the government seems to have gotten into difficulty and become inconsistent. There are both increases and decreases in duty, and the minister says the increases under the general tariff are small and that the material reductions in the British preferential rates are larges. It would be difficult at this time, and without further analysis, to say just exactly what will be the effect of these changes. The minister himself was not very definite or specific in that respect. These tariff items have been scrambled; they have been mixed up and re-arranged, and it will require some considerable time and the work of an expert to find out exactly what has happened. It is extremely difficult to unscramble eggs, and I think this government will have great difficult in unscrambling some of these complications which they have brought about. Some of the increases are very marked and some of the reductions are rather trifling.
I am particularly interested in the budget as it relates to agricultural products. We have had the case for the fruit and vegetable growers presented very fairly and completely by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), and I do not propose to go over the ground which he covered so well. It does appear, however, that the government has missed an opportunity to do something for this industry and has given it something which will not really help it. What these people really desired was a seasonal tariff or a rigid application of the dumping duty, and this does 2419-130
not appear to have been given them. However, I wish to deal very briefly with the Australian and New Zealand treaties, which materially affect the constituency which I represent, in which the dairy industry plays a very important part.
I am glad to recall that when this Australian treaty was discussed in this house I voted against it. I voted against it because it was clearly pointed out by my leader that its effects would be detrimental to agriculture, that while there would be some advantages to the manufacturing industry, agriculture would be called upon to pay for those advantages. The warnings then given, however, were disregarded, and it was not very long before the treaty was extended to New Zealand by order in council. That extension was made with disastrous results to the dairying industry of Canada. The operation of this treaty has destroyed the confidence, and the initiative of this industry; the industry is discouraged and downhearted. Every reason which exists at this late date for the termination of this treaty has existed and must have been well known to the government for many years. Why this delay and this tardy action? The action taken cannot give any benefit to the dairying industry for at least six months. After an industry has been damaged for six years, it cannot be rebuilt in six months; it will take years to bring it back to where it was at the time this government embarked upon the policy which wrought such havoc and which has brought such disaster to this industry. The government seeks now to take that action which it has been repeatedly requested to take.
The countervailing duties are a comparatively new feature in the customs tariff. Heretofore Canada has had the courage and the initiative to make her own tariffs, and parliament in making those tariffs has done so in the best interests of the Canadian people, without in any way playing second fiddle or waiting for the action of any other country. The adoption of this principle will result in confusion and uncertainty. The United States have a tariff law under which the president may on the recommendation of the tariff commission increase or decrease the rates of duty. This is called the flexible provision, and we shall have to follow that country up and down the whole scale from day to day if we are to put into force the countervailing duties referred to in the budget. Not only will there be changing rates from time to time with respect to the United States, but it will apply to other countries



The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
as well. The member for Southeast Grey points out that this countervailing feature applies only to sixteen items; and I wonder why it was not extended to a much larger number of items. During the past seven years the flexible provision in the tariff of the United States has been extremely detrimental to Canada. Canada has felt the effect of an increase of from 30 to 42 cents per bushel on wheat; from 75 cents to $1.04 per 100 pounds on flour; from S cents to 12 cents per pound on butter; from 1 cent to 14 cents per pound on onions; from 2J cents to 3-f cents per gallon on fresh milk; from 20 cents to 30 cents per gallon on cream, and increases on many other commodities. Every reason which has existed for the raising of the duty on these items has been in existence for the last eight years, ever since the Fordney-McCumber tariff was introduced in the United States in the year 1922. In spite of that, this government has slept and has allowed these changes to work to the detriment of Canada. At this late date, on the eve of an election, it comes forward with this feeble and futile effort in the hope that it can satisfy the agricultural industry and the people on the farms of Canada. I suggest that it is long too late and that the government will be disappointed in the results obtained. What is required in Canada is a protective tariff of agriculture and industry generally determined by the Canadian people and in the interests of agriculture, industry and labour. In its tariff provisions the budget makes an attempt to travel in two opposite directions at the same time. That has been tried in the past by statemen and politicians, but it has always met with failure and I predict that failure will be the result in the present instance.
From the information I have been able to obtain, I have come to the conclusion that the number of items to be included in the British preference has been exaggerated, with a desire to make it appear that larger reductions are being made. Why was it necessary at this late stage to deal with this matter? We are to have an eoonomic conference this fall, and would it not have been well for Canada to enter that conference with free hands, with this whole subject open for discussion and for negotiation? Then we could hope to obtain preference for preference; we could hope to receive some advantage- countervailing advantage if you like-for the reductions which we offered. The foundation of trade and commerce is mutual advantage, but that seems to have been disregarded in this instance'. The object of this gesture is to give the government a little flag to wave 
in the coming campaign. It is not a big flag and it is not going to be large enough to carry the government through, because side by side with it has to be carried the stars and stripes.
I was very much interested in the speech delivered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) at Woodstock. The hon. minister always makes a good speech, and with much of that speech, as reported in the Toronto Globe, I agree. He said that the Dunning budget was not a western budget-I agree with him in that statement. He said it was not an eastern budget-I am inclined to agree with him there. He said it was not a manufacturers' budget-I concur in that statement. He said it was not a farmers* budget-he is right. It was not a workingman's budget-he is absolutely right there. He said that it was a national budget with the great policy of British preference as its foundation-with that sentence I disagree, for the reasons I have already stated. It is not a national budget because it fails to give proper consideration to national interests. It is not determined entirely by the Canadian people; it is uncertain and variable in its action; it is, I suggest, a King government budget by the King government and for the King government and its whole object is to put the government out of the bog of despair and difficulty of its own making, in which it has landed itself and for which it has been heading for the last six or seven years.
Generally in matters of this kind we have uniformity, unanimity of opinion among the different members of the cabinet. We have sitting in that cabinet the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Crerar), and I have sat in the house and heard him session after session denounce protection as unsound, vicious and injurious to all classes of the Canadian people. How can that man remain a member of a cabinet or government that repudiates, that denies the truth of all the statements which he has ever made when he was in the house with respect to the Canadian tariff? We have the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who has taken a similar position. How can he vote for the budget? He has not explained the reasons or whether he has any reasons why he has changed his opinion. The Minister of Finance himself has scarcely given us any good reason for his remarkably sudden conversion in this matter. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) ridiculed a brick-for-brick tariff, ridiculed the contention that the Australian and New Zealand treaties were doing any injury to the agricultural industry of this country and said

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
that it would be folly to raise duties. How can he vote for the budget? The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) not long ago in discussing this matter in the house announced that the effect of raising the duty on butter would leave the farmer in a worse condition than at present. How does he justify the duties that are imposed and the countervailing duties that apply in this respect?
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has always said that the tariff was a tax and he has frequently proclaimed in the most vehement terms that the policy of his government was a downward and still downward revision of the tariff. He has taken the opportunity in other budget debates to show the progress that has been made along that line and he fervently pledged himself and his government to continue along those lines. But to-night we find that he has reversed that position and he is now proposing to the house an increased measure of protection. With further reference to the statement of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) with regard to what occurred at the peace conference as to the reduction of duties, may I read from Hansard of 1928 the statement of the Prime Minister in the budget debate;
May I say just one further word in regard to the method by which the government has proceeded in the matter of tariff revision. I doubt if the government's method could be better described than as set forth in the resolution which was passed at the inter-parliamentary conference held in Paris on August 25, last year. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred to a resolution adopted by the League of Nations. That resolution laid stress on the importance of nations reducing rather than raising their customs tariff. We are proud of the fact that Canada stands out as the one country in the world that has pursued the course which was there advocated by all of them. In connection with the inter-parliamentary conference-which I understand is an inter-parliamentary conference of all the nations in the world-the following resolution was passed:
The twenty-fourth inter-parliamentary conference regrets to note a general tendency among the states to raise their customs tariffs. It recommends that the national groups shall endeavour to arrest and to reverse that tendency.
Another of the Paris recommendations completes this one by expressing the wish "that methods of abolishing, or at least progressively and gradually reducing customs duties, be made an object of study in all countries	"
The report goes on to say that such annual reduction could be sufficiently slight not to cause a crisis and to permit the different national industries to adapt themselves to the new conditions.
That was the position of the Prime Minister a year ago. Hs was commending a reduction 2419-13ti
of tariff. To-day by his budget he must approve the raising of the tariff. That, however, is perhaps not difficult for him and he must justify his own position.
My time is almost up and I propose to give some reasons why I am going to vote against the budget. I will vote against the budget:
1.	Because a vote for it is an endorsement of hypocrisy and deception in political policies, and hypocrisy and deception are no more excusable in matters political than in others.
2.	Because it does not accurately and fully disclose the national finances or the prospective revenues for the current fiscal year.
3.	Because the extension of the British preference on the eve of an economic conference of the empire is premature, inopportune and possibly detrimental to the promotion of inter-imperial trade on the sound basis of mutual preference.
4.	Because the adoption of countervailing duties introduces uncertainty and instability into the tariff and will result in frequent changes, complications and inconsistencies in our tariff schedules.
5.	Because the record of this government on fiscal matters is so unstable and inconsistent that it cannot be relied upon to carry out in full measure the features of the budget which may appear to be commendable.
0. Because it is really a deathbed repentance and repudiation of its former pledges and policies.
7.	Because it does not afford sufficient protection for the textile industries.
8.	Because the measure of protection afforded to the branches of agriculture and dairying is belated and inadequate.
9.	Because it does not contain provisions for promoting the manufacture in Canada of a larger amount of our own natural resources.
10.	Because it does not contain ample provisions to afford relief for unemployment.
Then we have the amendment which was moved by my leader and which will be found on Hansard at page 1834. It reads:
That while this house welcomes and approves of every measure that will afford to Canadian agriculture, industry, and labour an equal opportunity and fair competition in the development of the rich and varied natural resources of the Dominion, and provide for the extension of inter-empire trade by mutually advantageous preferences and agreements, with due regard in either ease, to the interests of consumers, it is of opinion that the proposals which were submitted by the Minister of Finance on May 1st, are in several important respects so completely at variance with the policies of this government, as heretofore declared by its official leaders in parliament and elsewhere, that this administration having lost the confidence of the country, cannot safely be entrusted with
The Budget-Mr. Bock

the direction of the fiscal policy of Canada nor the carrying into effect of proposals to which it has heretofore been opposed and which constitute a breach of its solemn pledges to the electorate, and which are deceptive, fail to estimate the financial results of their operations and which create distrust of and contempt for representative institutions.
With every sentence and every sentiment there expressed I wholly agree, and I will vote for it because it exposes the defects and weakness and inconsistency of this government on its own record and its failure to discharge its whole duty to the people of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that I would be somewhat remiss if I did not contribute a few remarks to this budget debate. I wish in the first place to tender my hearty congratulations to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) both on his presentation of the budget and on the manner in which he has grappled with our tariff problems at a time when a man in his position might well have hesitated to take such courageous steps.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) in his address the other evening mentioned having presided at a meeting which the present Minister of Finance attended a good many years ago, where the hon. member for Mackenzie claimed to have prophesied at that time that Mr. Dunning had a great future ahead of him. His remarks recalled to my mind many occasions in the early days of the grain growers' association in Saskatchewan when we as delegates attended our annual convention of the organization, which was usually held at Regina, Moose Jaw or Saskatoon. The present Minister of Finance was always on hand at those meetings, first as a delegate, and later as a director and vice-president of the organization. Often when the subject under discussion seemed to be going round in circles, with amendments aud subamendments and so on, and when it seemed to be heading up a blind alley with everything in a mess, as Amos and Andy would say, the chairman or one of , the delegates would suggest that Charlie Dunning come in and unscramble the situation and put the assembly on their feet again. He was always able to clear the air, and the debate would be once more off to a good start. This was back in 1910 to 1914, when the present Minister of Finance was on the board of directors of that organization. Later he organized and had mflch to do with the direction of the destinies of the Saskatchewan Cooperative Elevator Company. This was an outstanding organization, and at the time of its purchase by the pool it had become the greatest grain handling firm on 
the continent. The hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Finance was always able to take care of any situation in which he was placed. It was sometimes said that he seemed to be a pinch hitter who was sent to bat whenever a tough situation cropped up. Later, when he became a member of the Saskatchewan legislature, he acted at different times as Minister of Railways, Provincial Treasurer, Minister of Telephones, Minister of Agriculture, and finally as Premier of the Province of Saskatchewan, and made good in every capacity. In 1926, when the federal department of railways was in need of reorganization, the Prime Minister sent him to bat when there were two down and the bases full. He got a three-bagger that time, for he had studied the Nelson terminal proposition. He switched the terminal from Nelson to Churchill, completed the line, and last year for the first time in the history of our government-owned roads, made the system pay. Now, once again we find him going to bat on the eve of an election, as Minister of Finance, in the second half of the last innings with the bases full and the score tied, and what does he do? Does he fall down? Nol He knocks the Hawley-Smoot pill, with its fancy tariff curves clear into the gulf of Mexico with a British preference bat, and I fancy I can see the fans sitting on the corral fences out west, reaching for their bull durham and saying, "Yes, Dunning made another home run."
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), referred to the budget this afternoon as spectacular. I think it was in order to term it spectacular as it was introduced by a very spectacular Minister of Finance. We westerners, of course, naturally feel proud of our Minster of Finance for we "saw him first", before he went into the big league, and I am confident that the western farmers who through the old grain growers' association helped him to acquire his economic education are still pulling for him as strong as ever, and when the Dominion championship series opens-it won't be long now-and the electors go to bat, they will judge the two great parties by their box score records of runs, hits and errors in the past, and there will be no doubt in their minds that they may safely trust the destinies of Canada to the party which has had the courage to face situations as they arise and readjust our tariff structures as changing world conditions may warrant, in spite of the howls of the opposition about losing their policy.
It is reassuring to note in this budget that there is a surplus of $44,500,000 and that about

The Budget-Mr. Bock
$80,000,000 is wiped from our national debt. This sets a new record and cuts the interest charges by over $4,000,000, and this in the face of increased expenditures of approximately $25,000,000 on capital account for taking care of such projects as the new Welland ship canal, the Hudson Bay railway, the St. Lawrence channel, harbour work at the lake heads, and public buildings in the city of Ottawa. So apparently there is nothing seriously wrong with this government.
One feature of our trade balance which was criticized by hon. gentlemen opposite was that Canada as a nation, like many of our citizens in the west as well as in the east, bought more goods than she sold this year, by about $103,000,000; and as our grain exports to the United Kingdom declined by $138,000,000 and our exports to Europe declined by $81,000,000, it only emphasizes the importance of our grain exports in maintaining favourable trade balances, and the urgent necessity of securing and holding the good will of all wheat importing countries of the world. We should then so arrange our tariffs as to make for freer interchange of goods for our grain and flour, and in my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker, the sweeping tariff reduction contained in this budget in the ratio of four decreases to one increase, particularly as they affect the British Empire, should go a long way towards restoring the good will of our best customer for Canadian grain.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) the other evening in his speech referred to the Minister of Finance as a Santa Claus unloading his bag of parcels which were not to be opened until after Christmas, or after the election. I may say that when the minister was enumerating the many items made free under the British preference, I also saw a picture of a Santa Claus with a pack as big as a load of hay; but I did not get the drift of the hon. member's remark "not to be opened until after the election," for with the tariff schedules and the trade statistics before him the hon. member could at least have opened some of them on the spot. Some of the parcels I think had their wrappers off when they arrived, and certainly there was one that was wide open. I refer to the tea package, because the very next day after the budget was brought down I saw in two Ottawa newspapers advertisements in big black letters that the price of tea had dropped 15 cents per pound.
The opposition members accused us of being bullied by the United States. They also talked about adopting red-blooded tactics. I think either the hon. member for Fort William or the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), or perhaps both of them, last session wanted us to remain here until the United States had come through with their tariff revision program in order that we might enact retaliatory measures. To-day in one breath they tell us we are inconsistent in introducing countervailing duties, and in the next breath they tell us we have not gone far enough in that direction. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said we ought to apply these countervailing duties to the tariff as a whole, that there were only a few items to which they were applied and these were not nearly enough. In fact, he referred to the limited number of items covered by the countervailing duties as the gesture of a school boy. I am sure if the genial member for Fort William prescribed a tablespoonful of castor oil to his colleague from Vancouver Centre, that gentleman would not insist on taking a whole quart of the medicine until he had found out how the first dose affected him.
Some of the Progressives appear to think that we have gone too far; the Tories think we have not gone far enough; but it appears to me as if we had sort of struck the happy medium, because when both hostile parties are dissatisfied in that way, from one extreme to the other, I think the Minister of Finance is not very far out in his proposals. As world conditions change it is necessary for governments to make alterations in their policies from time to time, to meet emergencies as they arise, that is, if we are going to make progress. It is said that if a man were to follow a beaten path continuously he would soon get into a rut. Well, there is only one difference between a rut and a grave -the rut has no ends to it.
There is a strong possibility, Mr. Speaker, that the United States government, after they have studied the effects of these countervailing duties on their own producers and consumers, may not hesitate very long to make some reductions in their tariff structure. In fact I think they have already made reductions in duties on shingles, lumber and potatoes, following the budget announcement. Press reports state that President Hoover is being deluged with requests to veto the tariff bill now before the congressional committee. So we may be pleasantly surprised by the effect that our countervailing duties may have on the tariff policies of our neighbours.
Taking the different factors into consideration, then, we have on the one hand Uncle Sam's attitude of closing his doors to many of our products by the proposals contained
The Budget-Mr. Bock

in the Hawley-Smoot tariff bill; and on the other hand we have a good market in Great Britain for our commodities, but. she is reluctant to purchase them unless we take in exchange those articles which we have been purchasing in the United States. When the Hudson Bay railway is in operation, which will be in the near future, it will have the effect of lowering our freight rates, thereby reducing our cost of production, which is one thing we should not lose sight of; and the trade diverted from the United States to Great Britain should help to provide cargoes for the wheat earners returning to Fort Churchill. So it seems to me that this budget is piecing those problems together like the parts of a jigsaw puzzle. The Minister of Finance has been a good solver of puzzles in the past, by the time he gets through with this puzzle there will be no pieces left over for my hon. friends opposite to play with.
Fundamentally I have always been just as much a free trader as my friend from Rose-town (Mr. Evans), but there are times when certain things cannot all be done at once owing to extraordinary conditions. If our natural north and south channels of trade nre obstructed, we can blame Uncle Sam and his tariff measures. If he thinks it good business to lose a few hundred million dollars worth of Canadian trade annually it is his own affair. And if his prohibitory tariff machine backfires too much on him, he will probably take it to the garage to have it overhauled; apparently he has changed the timing on his potatoes, lumber and shingles. I believe in the feasibility of the Hudson Bay railway as a grain shipping route, and I think our present difficulties will be removed with the opening of that route; and with the progress made by this budget towards free trade within the empire, it should only be a few years before the last barrier to imperial free trade has been removed.
I am convinced that the record of the present administration, together with the budget now under discussion, which appears so effectively to meet the peculiar trade conditions to-day, should return this government to power with an increased majority at the coming elections. The opposition apparently have no policy to offer that would deal effectively with the situation. They criticize every action of the government, but after listening to their speeches it is pretty hard to arrive at what the majority of them really favour. Some of them are of the opinion that the increased British preference would put our manufacturers out of business; some of them 
claim it has not gone far enough; in the opinion of others it should have come sooner. The same diversity of view exists with regard to the countervailing duties. In a word, the opposition have no clear-cut, definite policy to offer to the country. They may make an issue of having their shirt stolen, for they always have a slogan, something easy for the people to remember. I recall in 1011 they had the slogan "No annexation, no truck or trade with the Yankees;" in 1921 the slogan was "blue ruin"	in 1925 they
had another "blue ruin" slogan; in 1926 they had some more "blue ruin" together with the customs scandal. But this time they will not be waving the flag so effectively as they did in 1911. In Saskatchewan they are apparently raising a religious issue. It seems a pity that an election cannot be fought cleanly on a national policy without introducing questions of race, language or religion, for these appeal mostly to those who are little concerned with the real welfare of Canada. In this connection, sir, I should like to read an extract from a verbatim report of a speech made by the editor of the Regina Daily Star, which appears in the issue of his paper of May 2. The meeting was held in the town of Shaunavon which is in the Maple Creek constituency that I have the honour to represent. On that occasion a Conservative candidate was elected to contest the coming election, and the Hon. Mr. Bennett was chosen honorary president and Hon. Mr. Anderson honorary vice-president of the local association. I shall not attempt to quote the speech in full for it is rather lengthy, but it contains some passages which I feel it my duty to bring to the attention of hon. members. Among other statements made on that occasion by Mr. Cowper, the editor of the Regina Daily Star, are the following:
Canada to-day is facing a conflict between the two races. Only folly would blind one's eyes to it, and cowardice seal one's lips. The Quebec movement thriving on the liberty accorded to the Quebec people by the act of 1774 and generous concessions since extended to it by Canadian leaders has now reached a point where it seeks to effect the mental conquest of all Canada. In has put six ministers into the King government; it has utilized its solid bloc to control the Liberal caucus and party, so that to-day its minority in the house is in control of Canada. It has abused its power thus obtained to flout the constitution and is now actively using the departments of government and the federal civil service in a campaign to overthrow the British conceptions of democracy and freedom in Canada, to block the wrork of those who wish to weld all the peoples of Canada into a homogeneous Canadian nationhood. It is using its control of the

The Budget-Mr. Bock
post office, the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and other departments of the Ottawa government to force the French language on the peoples of the British provinces.
This is not an issue of this man or that; it is not a fight between the ins and the outs. The Quebec French movement by its control of the present government of Canada has thrown down the challenge to the people of the western provinces. The future destiny of Canada, the character of its democracy, the treasures of mental and spiritual liberty, are bound up in the issue. They constitute a clarion call to all lovers of mental liberty and national freedom to unite and defeat the King government, and keep the Quebec movement from riding roughshod over the heritage of our dearly loved British liberties.
That would seem to outline the main issue in the coming campaign in the section of Saskatchewan from which I come. This represents the opening gun which was fired at the nomination meeting of the Conservative candidate in the constituency of Maple Creek. As the hon. leader of the opposition has been named honorary president of this Conservative organization, I am sorry he is not in his seat, but I wonder if he agrees with the report which I have just read. I wonder if he endorses the statements that were made at that meeting; I doubt very much if he does. I do not believe that the hon. leader of the opposition is the type of man that will endorse the sentiments contained in this article. It is rumoured in Saskatchewan that the leader of the opposition has either directly or indirectly some financial interest in the Regina Star, from which newspaper I have just read. I do not know whether that is a correct statement or not, but at some future time I would like to have an answ'er from the hon. member. Judging from reports which I have seen in newspapers as to the stand taken by the hon. leader of the opposition in connection with stirring up religious strife, I believe he is too big a man to countenance that sort of thing. I would like to read an article which appeared in the Western Producer in its issue of July 5, 1928. The newspaper heading is as follows;
Hon. R. B. Bennett speaks of policies of Tory party to French Canadians.
This address was delivered at Magog, in the province of Quebec, and in part is as follows:
He who makes appeal to prejudice, racial or religious, is a foe to Canada. Let by-gones be by-gones; study matters for yourselves, and when you go to the polls do not go as men and women driven by passion or prejudice, but strike a blow for the preservation of your country and its institutions, and an opportunity for development.
In dealing with the manner in which the hon. gentleman was received, the report is as follows:
"You receive me like a son just returned home," laughingly remarked Mr. Bennett in reply to the applause which greeted him when he rose to speak. He went on to talk of the necessity of not thinking only in terms of one province, but of all Canada, and preached his doctrines of peace and unity. As to appeals which have been made in Quebec against the Conservative party, he said the party would prefer defeat rather than deny the rights of minorities. "This party will go into ignom-inous defeat and cease to exist before it will tolerate doing away with any of your rights," he declared.
On June 24, 1928, at Laprairie, Quebec, Mr. Bennett paid tribute to the work of French Canadians in building up Canada and regretted he could not deliver his speech in the beautiful French tongue. On that occasion his speech was reported as follows by the Canadian Press:
"We must respect the rights of the minority whether in this province, Prince Edward Island or any other province," Mr. Bennett declared in recalling that the Conservative party under Sir John A. Macdonald had suffered defeat in protecting the rights of the minority.
"This Canada of ours must go forward without any dividing line of race, creed or religion, and in this course lies our salvation," he declared. The British North America Act which protected the right of the French minority could not be lightly set aside, he asserted.
These two articles do not very well coincide; they would seem to correspond about as well as the triangle and the circle, if I might be permitted to use that example. I hope that if the leader of the opposition has any control over the Conservative organizations in Saskatchewan he will put the brakes on that particular brand of politics.
I was pleased to note the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) as they appear in Hansard on April 29. On that occasion he took exception to newspaper editorials and clippings from the Regina Daily Star containing attacks on the Roman Catholic church, and apparently he was very much concerned with these newspaper articles. I am heartily in accord with him in his condemnation of that disrupting and un-Canadian style of politics. At this time I would like to read a few remarks of the hon. gentleman on that occasion. He said:
I have a considerable number of constituents, probably one-half, who are of the Roman Catholic faith, and a considerable number of those are of the French Canadian race. I find circulated amongst those people newspaper editorials, small excerpts reprinted from the Regina Star and other papers containing
The Budget-Mr. Bock

attacks upon the Roman Catholic faith that I, from my training, breeding and education, could certainly never endorse. I find those being circulated in my constituency among my electors, as providing a reason why I should not be returned to parliament from that constituency, simply because I am alleged to be in some sort of a conspiracy with the Saskatchewan government, of whose very composition I am ignorant, to wipe out the Catholic church and to make the Ku Klux Klan supreme in that province. I say to the right hon. gentleman and to those of his supporters who manipulate such propaganda, that if that is continued I am prepared to go throughout the length and breadth of the province of Quebec and tell the people, as I am telling him to-day, that the restricted rights and privileges of the Roman Catholic minority in those prairie provinces are in a large measure due to the terms of the constitutional acts of 1905 which were amended in committee by the government of which Sir Wilfrid was leader, in order to gain for his government an increased support in the English speaking provinces in which the Protestants had a majority. I now say to my hon. friend that if we are to avoid these discussions in my constituency and in the surrounding constituencies, they must at least avoid attributing to me any persistent hostility to the Roman Catholic faith-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To get back to the question of the British preference, I must say that I listened with considerable interest to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). I noticed that he seemed to take very keen delight in abusing and ridiculing everything in connection with this budget and the Liberal party generally. I was much impressed by the vigorous manner in which this hon. gentleman unloaded his logic. Probably I should use the word language rather than logic. While I had previously held the opinion that the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) was entitled to the belt for rapid-fire oratorical efforts, I am afraid that hon. gentlemen had better look to his laurels because in my opinion the hon. member for Fort William almost eclipsed the record of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest. It would be interesting to have an endurance contest staged between these two hon. gentlemen. I would suggest that Mr. Speaker might donate an oratorical challenge cup to be competed for in open competition. I would venture to say that if my hon. friend the leader of the opposition did not win it himself it would be captured by either the hon. member for Fort William or the hon. member for Toronto Northwest. In the opening remarks of the hon. member for Fort William he stated that he could not understand anything contained in the budget, yet he followed that remark by a criticism which was more 
extensive in character than the criticisms of any other half dozen members combined. His remarks reminded me of a character in Mark Twain's "Huckleberry Finn." Huckleberry Finn's father was said to have been the champion cusser of the entire neighbourhood, and hi3 devoted son "Huckleberry" being very proud of his old dad, boasted that his parent could cuss faster and more effectively thant any other man in the community. He elaborated upon his father's ability by saying the the elder Finn could begin by cussing his closest neighbour, and from that point would include all the residents of the village, cussing them individually and collectively in a most efficient manner. Then he would widen the compass of his maledictions to include the adjoining neigh-hood, and he would cuss in particular any person of outstanding importance. After he had completed that category he would take in the senators, judges, congressmen and everyone in authority, always winding up with the president of the United States. He would give the president a thorough cussing and then, for fear he might have overlooked someone, would start with the president once more and go backwards, cussing them all over again. If Huckleberry Finn's father was the champion cusser of the United States I think the hon. member for Fort William might qualify as the champion vituperator, if I might use the word, of the House of Commons, for apparently he took a leaf out of Mr. Finn's Book and retraced his steps to make sure that no member of the government had been neglected.
However, from what I could gather from the occasional drift of reason which could be discerned through his barrage of ridicule I could catch no glimpse of the policy the hon. gentleman would suggest as a substitute for the policy he was criticizing so severely. He did, however, live up to a prediction made by his leader the other day in speaking in Guelph at the nomination meeting of the hon. member for South Wellington, when he said that all converts could be relied upon to make a mess of things. After listening to the speech of the hon. gentleman-of course, he may not be a 100 per cent convert; he may be only a backslider-I was reminded of an occasion during the campaign of 1926, in my own constituency. During that year the Tories fought their campaign with practically no ammunition except the customs scandal and blue ruin; at least that was the case in the west whatever it might have been in the east. They talked customs scandal and blue ruin exclusively in my part of the country.

The Budget-Mr. Bock
The leader of the opposition honoured the town of Shaunavon with a visit, during which he addressed a large audience in the local theatre on behalf of the candidate for the Maiple Creek constituency. This was the same candidate who was nominated just a couple of weeks ago, at the meeting during which the editor of the Regina newspaper made his startling oration. The leader of the opposition was the main speaker at that meeting, of course, and he had a good audience; the hall was filled. He was in good shape that night; and did not have any trouble at all in speaking and was not embarrassed by any means. This was the first time I had ever seen the leader of the opposition, and I had driven many miles to see him. Of course I did not meet the hon. gentleman, but I was amazed at the way he unloaded conversation. He lambasted the Liberal party wonderfully that night. He took the customs department all apart, tore the officials into shreds, and busted the government wide open. He took a couple of kicks at George Spence, the sitting member for the constituency; put Moses Aziz in gaol and threw away the key, and then took us all for a ride on some boat called the Maggie, or the Margaret. He showed us a wonderful time, and all admitted he was a great speaker. He had language to burn and he burned plenty of it.
After the leader of the opposition had burned up the government pretty successfully, he mentioned that the Tory party was going to safeguard everybody, although he did not say much about protection. He said a vote for the Tory candidate was going to pave highways to happiness, as I remember it, and with little talk of tariff or any other policy he had us just about convinced that if his party was elected it would turn us from bankruptcy to prosperity over night, and that this-would happen if only we would get aboard his political band wagon. After he had mopped his perspiring brow and the dust had settled down a bit, he informed the electors that if they wanted another spasm he could turn on some more, but intimated that he would prefer to answer a few questions if any person cared to put them to him. No one volunteered for a moment to ask questions, because the audience were still more or less spellbound, finally a tall, rather tired looking fellow sitting down about the middle of the hall, who from his riding boots and general appearance looked as though he might have come in from some ranch, got to his feet and in a mild tone of voice asked the chairman if the speaker would tell him something
about the policy of the Tory party. A solemn hush fell upon that meeting; you could almost hear the chairman gulp as he nearly swallowed his Adam's apple. The man sitting next to the rancher edged away from him as though embarrassed at being even close to a man who would ask a question, which was considered rather impertinent. However, the leader of the opposition rose to the occasion; he stepped to the front of the platform, fixed the questioner with his eagle eye, pointed an accusing finger at him and, in a voice filled with scorn, repeated those well known words which I am sure many of us have heard him use. "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." About that time the audience caught their breath and heaved a sigh of relief. Apparently they had expected to see the inquisitive rancher wither right up in his boots, but to their amazement he never batted an eye; he replied to the leader of the opposition that he had come to the meeting to hear something about the policy of the Conservative party, but so far he had heard nothing but a tirade of abuse and ridicule directed against everything connected with the Liberal government. He said he had only asked that question because he was interested in learning what the opposition had to offer by way of a policy. Mr. Bennett [DOT]then rather amplified his previous explanation by stating that in his opinion he had been explaining the Conservative doctrine for more than an hour, and once more he said to that man: "He that hath ears to hear, and hear not; he that hath eyes to see and see not, it were better that a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were cast into the sea."
After he had so successfully disposed of this seeker for information the meeting broke up in the usual way, but there wTere many murmurs heard throughout the crowd because that inquisitive rancher appeared to have started a new train of thought in the minds of the audience and when the campagn was over the candidate on whose behalf the leader of the opposition had spoken was defeated by Hon. George Spence by between 2,000 and 3,000 of a majority. So it appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that something more than ridicule and abuse will be necessary during this coming election. They will require something more definite in the way of a national policy than they have yet revealed, if they expect to attain even a percentage of that success which the most optimistic among them are predicting.
The Budget-Mr. Hanson

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Bock) will not accuse me of discourtesy if I do not attempt to follow him in the various lines of his discourse. It has been well said that every circus must have its clown, and we all realize the truth of that saying now. Least of all do I wish to follow him in the fulsome flattery which he has heaped upon his former provincial leader, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). Attention should however be drawn to that reference which he made to my leader in relation to national unity. My leader has been before the public of this Dominion many years and I have never heard it asserted that he has been a disruptor of national unity. On the contrary, I say, and without fear of successful contradiction, that upon every occasion he has been the defender of national unity and of the constitutional rights and liberties of the minority races in this country.
All of us who listened to the pronouncement of the Minister of Finance on May 1 have been wondering just what has come over the spirit of the Liberal party. I have been a member of this house for nearly nine sessions, and it has been instilled into my brain that the policy of the parry now in powe was just the reverse of the underlying intent of the budget presented this year. Throughout the whole history of the Liberal party, especially when elections were in the offing, there have been sudden conversions, and there have been at least two or three similar budgets presented during the nine years I have been a member of this house. When the government's ear was to the ground, and when the electors were making known their disapproval of government policy, the Liberal party always has run true to form and has not hesitated to depart from its traditional principles on the eve of the vote taking. The Minister of Finance must have been placed in an ironical position in delivering this budget, having regard to his previous political commitments both in and out of this house, and especially in view of the statements made upon his first platform appearance in the city of Regina. I regret that due to domestic illness the hon. minister has been prevented from being present during the whole of this debate. In that regard I am sure he has the sympathy of every member of this house. But while there may be ample excuse for the absence of the Minister of Finance, there is absolutely no excuse for the absence from this chamber during this debate of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar). In the name of the people of

this country I say to the Minister of Railways that it will not do for him to shirk attendance at this debate; he must rise to his feet during the course of this discussion and justify if he can his present political position, having regard to his previous history. The country, and especially the province of Manitoba will be satisfied with nothing less than an explanation either of his conversion or of his recantation.
There is considerable in this budget which warrants careful study and analysis, as I do not believe that any hon. member in listening to the announcements in the budget speech was able to grasp the full importance of the various sections and provisions. It would be strange indeed if any announcement of policy did not contain some good points. There are some points in this budget worthy of the careful consideration of the people of this country and of the members of this house, but those points which do not meet the fiscal conditions at present obtaining in this country are worthy only of the condemnation of the people of Canada. I venture to assert that most of the first-blush verdicts which have been made in respect to this budget will be reversed after a final analysis has been made. Especially is that true with respect to those parts of the budget which are protectionist or which have to do with the application of the British preference.
I have not the time at my disposal to go into a detailed analysis of the provisions of the iron and steel schedule of the budget. I must confess that this is a technical matter and only those well versed in the technicalities of the steel industry are able to pronounce judgment upon it. It would be presumptuous on my part to attempt to make a detailed analysis or to express any final judgment or conclusion. However, I feel sure that we will not obtain the full measure of benefits which I have no doubt the Minister of Finance and the ministry generally sincerely desired should accrue as a result of the changed schedules. The underlying intent in the revision of the steel and iron schedule and of the British preference was to transfer in a degree-just how much we have not been told-a portion of the import business in iron and steel either to this country or to the old country If that is the honest intent of the ministry, I have no quarrel to make because ever since this party came into power in 1921 the business of this country has degenerated to a large degree into the hands of our neighbours to the south. Any reasonable measure which will transfer business from the United States to Canada, or failing to Canada

The Budget-Mr. Hanson
then to the old country, per se merits our very sincere support. Whether or not this budget will have that effect upon the iron and steel business of this country I do not feel competent to say; I can only express the opinions of others who I believe know what the conditions are. The well considered judgment of gentlemen who should be in a position to judge of this matter is that with respect to certain of the heavier iron and steel commodities there will be a substantial reversal of the present trade conditions, but with respect to other features of the iron and steel trade there will be substantially no difference. In so far as the government has not gone far enough .to effect the desired result, the government is to blame.
The budget, as has been said this afternoon, naturally divides itself into three major aspects: the question of the revision of the tariff schedules, the question of the extension of the British preference, and the adoption of the system of countervailing duties, which is, I understand, not exactly a new departure, but which has been put into effect at least by the Liberal party for the first time. I shall not attempt to deal further with the affirmative features of the first aspect of the budget, but before I resume my seat I desire to say a word or two from the opposite standpoint and I suppose I might do so at this point as well as later on. I want to confess to great disappointment that on the eve of a general election the government has not done something more for Canadian industry and labour. That is a very general statement and I should, I suppose, particularize.
I have in mind two industries in my own immediate community. One is a branch of the cotton industry and the other is related to the boot and shoe industry. I must at once take issue with the remark of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Maophail) that there should have been any extension of the British preference with reference to boots and shoes or cottons. I would say to her: "Have a heart," and I would take her gently by the hand, lead her down to my community, and show her, because there is an old adage that seeing is believing. I would take her to a beautiful little town situated three miles from my own city where away back in 1882 one of the great pioneers of the Dominion established with his own money, with the foresight which was characteristic of him, a great industry in order that the people of that community and country might live at home and not have to go abroad to earn their living. It is true that the industry which he established was not, in the language

of some of our free trade friends, indigenous to the country; but at all events he was a man of vision, and there he built of brick, mortar and machinery what was at that time the largest cotton mill in the Dominion of Canada, and which stands to-day as practically the only monument to his memory. That industry has been going on under one ownership or another until the present day. But let me tell the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) who, I believe, is very solicitous for his friends in the boot and shoe trade, that never before in the history of the cotton industry has there been such depression, yes, despair, as there is to-day. I would show the hon. member for Southeast Grey a beautiful little community with a single industry employing in normal times 800 well paid, happy contented artisans, maintaining a happy population of more than 2,000 souls who, in turn, buy the entire produce of the surrounding country. To-day, would you believe it, as a result of the changes that have been made, not this year but in previous years, by the present government, those people have been reduced so that within the last few months they have been working just three days a week. That has meant all the difference between a happy, contented community and one that is just on the border line of poverty. One of the complaints I have against the budget is that no relief has been afforded for the textile industry. I believe I could duplicate in Quebec, the province of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, the picture which I am endeavouring to paint in the house tonight, and I can duplicate and more than duplicate it in other sections of my own province.

It can be increased one
hundredfold in the province of Quebec.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I could take the hon. member for Southeast Grey down to the city of St. John where years ago two cotton mills were built by one family and where to-day we have the announcement that one of those mills is to be closed permanently, to the loss of the industrial life of the whole community and to the especial loss of the people engaged in that industry. I am not particularly concerned with the stockholders of Canadian Cottons Limited. The friends of the Minister of Justice situated in the city of Montreal, and especially his friend in the Senate, no doubt have had something to say about that from the standpoint of the shareholders of the company. But let me say this on their behalf: I believe it is a very well managed institution, but for the first time in many years they have just passed their common
The Budget-Mr. Hanson

dividend and I understand only from to-day's paper that the statement of last year is so bad that the dividend on the preferred shares, that is the outstanding shares of that company preferred as to dividends, upon which shares they rely very largely for their borrowed capital, is in danger of being passed and I have no doubt will be passed. I make a special plea on behalf, not of the shareholders of this corporation or of any other manufacturing corporation, but of the thousands of men and women of this country who have been deprived of a decent livelihood by virtue of the policy of attrition adopted by the government in the last nine years in respect to the textile industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The same thing obtains in the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The same thing does not obtain in the United States, and the hon. member does not know what he is talking about.
I am glad to know that the boot and shoe industry has a noble champion in the person of the hon. member for Quebec East, the present Minister of Justice, but I want to put it to him that it is not fair to increase the British preference on boots and shoes to the detriment of our own industry. I yield to no one in my loyalty to the empire; that loyalty has been paid for in blood, but I say to him that in the exercise of the power of extension of the British preference every care should be taken by the government not to injure a presently existing Canadian industry. The boot and shoe industry in this country, especially in the higher class grades of men's boots, is just shivering on the brink of disaster and any further extension of the British preference with respect to boots and shoes will mean the closing up of all the high class factories in the Dominion. I am sure that if the Minister of Justice will investigate the matter he will find from his own friends that that statement is not far astray.
Unconsciously, Mr. Speaker, I have drifted from the first aspect of this budget to the second. I do not intend to labour further on the question of the British preference, because I believe that we can illustrate the dangers of the extension of the principle of the British preference by concrete examples better than in any other way.
Just one word more with respect to the boot and shoe industry. Boots and shoes made in my home city and in the cities of the province of Quebec are to-day selling in the retail stores throughout Canada in competition with boots and shoes made in Northampton, England. On the surface I have no

quarrel with that, nor would I have if the two industries, the one located in this country and the other in the old land, were on an exact parity. But they are not, and unless the standards of living and all labour conditions in the old land change, they never will be on an exact parity. In other words, the standard of living of the boot and shoe operators in our Canadian cities is away above and beyond the standard of living of similar operators in Northampton, England. Now unless we are going to adopt the position that we ought not to have this industry at all in this country, or the alternative position that we want the standard of living of our boot and shoemakers in this country lowered to the standard of living in the old land, and working conditions here comparable with the conditions obtaining in Northampton, England, our boot and shoe industry, unless something is done, has got to go down, and I appeal to the Minister of Justice to stand pat on this question of the extension of the British preference with relation to boots and shoes. He has not seen fit to do it in this budget, and I fear very much for the future if the Minister of Justice should be translated elsewhere. I doubt very much, especially in view of the increasing ascendency of the free trade element in the Liberal party save and except as exemplified by this budget, whether the boot and shoe makers of this country would have on the other side of the house any champion if the Minister of Justice should go. So one of the chief faults that I have to find with this budget is what it does not contain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member be good enough to tell the house what change he would make in the tariff with regard to the boot and shoe industry?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me preface my answer by saying that I want to make it quite plain that I am expressing my own view. I would adopt such a policy as would stabilize the Canadian industry first, and before I went to any economic conference or considered the further extension of the principle of reducing the British preference I would make a thorough survey of the whole situation, and where I did not think the tariff high enough to start with, I would jack it up first and consider an extension of the preference afterwards. I would jack it up to such a point as to make it plain that I would allow no Canadian industry to suffer in unequal competition with British industry. That is my answer, and I would not be open to the charge of disloyalty either, because the Britisher is a man who plays fair and I think he would say that I was doing just what was right.

The Budget-Mr. Hanson

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that the policy of the Conservative party on this same item?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That opens up a very wide question. I took very great care to tell my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. Young), who is a friend of mine, I think, that I was speaking for myself. My leader is quite capable of speaking for himself on this or any other question. Further, let me say that if I have read aright the debates of this parliament in previous years I am simply reiterating in different form the doctrine of the late lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I want to address a few remarks to the question of countervailing duties. I am satisfied that the countervailing duties proposed in this budget are just a feeble gesture on the part of this government in answer to the attitude of the United States. It is nothing but a feeble gesture, and I have no doubt that it waill fall short of the intent of the minds which devised the suggestion. Every thoughtful Canadian-I do not think that this feeling is confined by any means to members of my own party, although I make bold to say that we first seized on the point and recognized it from the very beginning-has felt the danger of the gradual absorption of our trade by the United States. There has been in my own mind a lurking fear of the economic conquest of this country. The development of our trade with the United States, especially in manufactured goods, coupled with the attitude, not of the people of the United States but of the government of the United States, during the last eight years ever since the Fordney-MoCumber tariff came into operation, has been fraught with great danger to the economic life of this country. For eight years I have heard gentlemen representing the point of view which I support on this side of the house beg and plead with the present leader of this government (Mr. Mackenzie King) to take notice and some action with regard to that economic situation. Last session especially some of us on this side of the house begged the Prime Minister to take official notice of the action and attitude of the congress of the United States, but until the very eve of an election our pleadings have fallen on deaf ears. But now the great voice of the people willy-nilly has got across to this government, and I believe that there is nothing that the party opposite fears so much to-day as the attitude of shilly-shallying-I can find no better expression-on this great national problem which has characterized the Liberal party during the past eight years. I believe that the Prime Minister is alive to the danger, and he seeks to meet it by this countervailing
effort of his. In my 'humble judgment that effort will fall far short of its intent. In the first place the number of items to which the countervailing duties apply is far too low. I am not going to speak of the question of a brick for brick tariff. I am going to leave that to the Minister of Agriculture to chew over and reflect upon, especially in view of the way in which I have heard him pour ridicule year after year on my late leader. I want to say to the Minister of Agriculture that he along with his colleague the Minister of Railways will have to do some heartsearching. " I shall leave that to him. I want to treat this question, if I can, from a businesslike standpoint.
* This policy of countervailing duties will not in my humble judgment divert the trade that it is sought to divert; neither will the extension of the British preference nor the imposition of certain duties in the iron and steel schedules. If I understand present economic conditions, there is only one way to divert trade from the United States into the hands of our own producers or of our kinsmen across the sea, and that is to raise the duties on manufactured goods, or on other goods that we want to shut out, so high that our foreign competitors cannot send them here. Only in that way will you effectively divert trade from the United States to the British Empire in such commodities as we cannot manufacture here.
I am not at the moment seeking to do that. What I prefer is that we should firmly establish a fiscal policy that will build up this country first. That is the policy my leader has been preaching in season and out of season ever since appointment to his present high office, and that is the policy that the mass of the thinking people of Canada. the artisans and workers, desire. I know that the people in my own community are not so much concerned about the cost of certain articles as they are about having the money in their pockets to buy those articles. I should like that truth to sink into the hearts and souls of some of my free trade friends apposite, because I do not question their sincerity; I question their judgment. In this connection, sir, I believe that when the electorate have an opportunity to declare their views, they will speak in no uncertain tone.
